High Priest
hy preest
noun phrase (biblical office)
From Hebrew kohen gadol ("great priest") and kohen harosh ("chief priest"); Greek archiereus. The chief of the Aaronic priesthood, the one priest who entered the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement.

See also: High Priest

📖 Biblical Definition

The high priest (Hebrew kohen gadol, "great priest") was the chief of the Aaronic priesthood in Israel — the one man who, on the Day of Atonement, entered the Holy of Holies behind the veil to make atonement for the sins of the whole people. The office began with Aaron, the brother of Moses, and passed through his line. The high priest's distinctive garments (Exod 28) marked his unique office: the ephod, the breastplate of judgment bearing the twelve stones of the tribes over his heart, the Urim and Thummim, the blue robe with its bells and pomegranates, and the golden plate on his mitre engraved "HOLINESS TO THE LORD." He bore the names of the tribes before the LORD, representing the whole people. His supreme function was the annual Day of Atonement (Lev 16): once a year, and only the high priest, and not without blood, he entered the Most Holy Place to sprinkle the blood of the sin offering upon and before the mercy seat, making atonement for the sanctuary and the people. The entire institution was a shadow, designed by God to prepare His people for the substance: Jesus Christ, the great High Priest of the new covenant (Heb 4:14-16; 7-10). The Epistle to the Hebrews develops the comparison at length: Christ is a high priest after the order of Melchizedek, not Aaron; He is holy, harmless, undefiled, needing no sacrifice for His own sins; He entered not the earthly Holy of Holies but heaven itself; He offered not the blood of bulls and goats but His own blood; He made atonement not annually but once for all; and He ever lives to make intercession for His people. The earthly high priest who entered behind the veil once a year, trembling, with another's blood, pointed to the one High Priest who entered heaven once for all, by His own blood, and sat down. The veil that barred the way was torn at His death (Matt 27:51); through Him the believer now draws near with boldness (Heb 10:19-22).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The chief of the Aaronic priesthood (Hebrew kohen gadol), the one priest who entered the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16); his whole office a shadow of Jesus Christ, the great High Priest after the order of Melchizedek who entered heaven once for all by His own blood (Heb 4-10).

HIGH PRIEST, noun phrase. Hebrew kohen gadol ("great priest"); Greek archiereus; chief of the Aaronic priesthood.

Began with Aaron; the one man who entered the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16).

Distinctive garments (Exod 28): ephod, breastplate of judgment with the twelve tribal stones, Urim and Thummim, the mitre plate "HOLINESS TO THE LORD."

A shadow of Jesus Christ, the great High Priest after the order of Melchizedek (Heb 4:14-16; 7-10).

Christ entered heaven itself, by His own blood, once for all, and ever lives to make intercession; the veil was torn at His death (Matt 27:51).

📖 Key Scripture

Leviticus 16:32-34 — "And the priest, whom he shall anoint... shall make an atonement... And this shall be an everlasting statute unto you, to make an atonement for the children of Israel for all their sins once a year."

Hebrews 4:14-15 — "Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin."

Hebrews 9:11-12 — "But Christ being come an high priest of good things to come... by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us."

Hebrews 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The high priest is corrupted when read as mere ancient ritual office, when the office's typology of Christ is missed, or when the priesthood is wrongly perpetuated in a human sacrificing priesthood that obscures the one finished priesthood of Christ.

expand to see more

Typology-missed misreading. The high priest is not merely an interesting ancient office; the whole institution was designed by God as a shadow of Christ (Heb 8:5; 10:1). Every feature points: the one man who alone could enter God's presence, bearing the names of the people on his heart, entering only with blood, only once a year, only into a tent — all of it pointing to the one Mediator who alone brings men to God, bearing His people on His heart, entering by His own blood, once for all, into heaven itself. To read the high-priestly institution without seeing Christ is to read the shadow and miss the substance the shadow was cast to reveal.

Perpetuated-priesthood misreading. The Roman Catholic Mass rests on a sacrificing human priesthood that re-presents Christ's sacrifice at every altar — a perpetuation of the priestly office that the Epistle to the Hebrews directly forecloses. Hebrews insists that Christ's one offering was final ("by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified," Heb 10:14), that He sat down (the earthly priests stood, their work never done; Christ sat, His work finished, Heb 10:11-12), and that there remains no more offering for sin. The new covenant has one High Priest, Christ, and a priesthood of all believers under Him (1 Pet 2:9); it has no order of sacrificing human priests, for the one sacrifice has been offered once for all. To perpetuate a sacrificing priesthood is to obscure the finished priesthood of Christ that Hebrews exists to proclaim.
